Chapter 01 · Your first professional chapter

From qualification
to contribution.

A degree, diploma or professional qualification gives you a foundation. Your first role teaches you how to apply that foundation within a functioning organisation.

The transition begins when you understand that your work is no longer completed only for marks, grades or academic assessment. It becomes part of a wider system in which colleagues, departments, suppliers and customers may depend on your accuracy and reliability.

  • A calculation may influence a quotation.
  • A drawing may guide a manufacturing process.
  • An inspection report may determine whether a product is accepted.
  • A purchase decision may affect production continuity.
  • A production schedule may influence customer delivery.
  • A financial entry may affect management decisions.
  • A customer response may shape a long-term relationship.
Professional growth begins when you recognise the consequence of every task entrusted to you.
Team work

Every great career begins with the courage to contribute.

Chapter 02 · More than a first job

A foundation for the professional
you may become.

The purpose of a fresher opportunity should not be limited to filling an entry-level position. It should help young professionals understand:

  • How organisations convert ideas into outcomes
  • How departments operate as one interconnected system
  • How quality is planned, created, measured and protected
  • How customer requirements influence internal processes
  • How safety, confidentiality and integrity guide decisions
  • How communication affects execution
  • How individual discipline contributes to organisational reliability
  • How professional capability develops through consistent responsibility
Your first designation is only a starting point. The habits, standards and judgement you develop during your initial professional years can influence the direction of your entire career.
Chapter 03 · The transformation

From academic confidence
to professional competence.

Academic success demonstrates your ability to learn. Professional success requires you to apply knowledge consistently, responsibly and collaboratively.

01

Knowledge

Creates a foundation.

02

Exposure

Creates understanding.

03

Practice

Creates confidence.

04

Feedback

Creates improvement.

05

Responsibility

Creates maturity.

06

Consistency

Creates professional credibility.

You are not expected to know everything when you join. You are expected to learn, ask responsible questions, accept guidance, improve continuously and become increasingly dependable.
Chapter 04 · Your first 100 days

A structured beginning
to a long-term career.

The first few months of employment can shape how confidently and effectively a young professional enters the workplace.

01–07
Days 01–07

Understand the environment

Complete joining formalities, workplace orientation, safety training, product introduction and departmental familiarisation. Learn how your role contributes to the organisation.

08–30
Days 08–30

Build the foundation

Understand basic processes, documents, systems, reporting relationships and performance expectations. Observe experienced colleagues and complete guided assignments.

31–60
Days 31–60

Begin contributing

Support defined responsibilities, prepare documentation, participate in discussions and apply academic concepts to practical work.

61–90
Days 61–90

Demonstrate reliability

Complete recurring responsibilities with improving accuracy, communicate progress clearly and begin identifying problems independently.

100
Day 100

Review your development

Discuss strengths, improvement areas, learning progress, role understanding and objectives for the next stage.

The first 100 days are not intended to test whether you already know everything. They are intended to establish whether you can learn, adapt, communicate and develop into a dependable professional.
Chapter 05 · The graduate development journey

From first exposure
to role ownership.

01

Orientation — Enter the organisation

Understand the company, workplace culture, safety requirements, product range, customers, policies and professional conduct expectations.

02

Functional learning — Understand your department

Learn your department's objectives, processes, documents, responsibilities, performance measures and relationship with other functions.

03

Guided contribution — Apply your knowledge

Complete supervised assignments, operational tasks, analysis, reporting or project activities.

04

Independent responsibility — Own defined work

Take responsibility for clearly established deliverables, timelines, quality standards and communication requirements.

05

Performance development — Improve your capability

Use feedback, training, observation and experience to reduce errors, increase confidence and strengthen decision-making.

06

Cross-functional awareness — Understand the larger system

Gain exposure to related departments and understand how decisions move across the organisation.

07

Specialisation and growth — Build your direction

Develop deeper technical, commercial, operational or managerial expertise based on capability, interest and organisational requirements.

Training

Learning through real work.

Chapter 06 · Fresh thinking meets experience

Where young professionals learn from generations of knowledge.

Freshers enter the workplace with recent academic knowledge, new perspectives, digital familiarity, ambition and curiosity.

Experienced professionals contribute practical judgement, process understanding, customer awareness and lessons developed through years of responsibility.

At Pradako, professional development grows through this exchange.

An experienced engineer may explain why a manufacturing process has evolved in a particular way. A machine operator may demonstrate why setup discipline influences product consistency. A quality professional may show how a minor deviation can affect customer acceptance. A purchase professional may explain how supplier performance affects production. A finance professional may demonstrate how operational decisions influence cost and cash flow. A young professional may introduce a digital tool, analytical method or new perspective.

Knowledge should not simply be transferred. It should be understood, questioned responsibly, improved and carried forward.

Chapter 07 · Learn the complete system

Your department is important.
The organisation is interconnected.

No function operates in isolation.

  • Production depends on materials, tools, people, planning, maintenance and quality.
  • Quality depends on drawings, specifications, measurement systems, process discipline and documentation.
  • Purchase depends on technical requirements, supplier capability, cost, quality and delivery.
  • Sales depends on manufacturing capability, costing, communication and customer confidence.
  • Finance depends on accurate operational and commercial information.
  • Supply chain connects customer demand, procurement, inventory, production and delivery.
Young professionals are encouraged to understand not only what their department does, but also how it supports the final result.

Chapter 09 · A role with real responsibility

Learn through work
that matters.

Freshers may begin by supporting experienced team members, but development should gradually lead to meaningful responsibility. Depending on the role, assignments may include:

  • Preparing production or operational reports
  • Reviewing drawings and specifications
  • Supporting process studies
  • Assisting with inspection and testing
  • Analysing quality or performance data
  • Coordinating with suppliers
  • Preparing purchase comparisons
  • Supporting customer documentation
  • Updating ERP or digital systems
  • Preparing costing information
  • Tracking delivery commitments
  • Participating in improvement projects
  • Conducting market or industry research
  • Supporting audits and compliance activities
  • Preparing presentations and management reports
  • Studying recurring problems and possible root causes
  • Documenting processes and standard operating procedures
The objective is not to keep freshers permanently limited to assistance. The objective is to build the competence required for independent contribution.
Chapter 10 · Short-term goals

Strong careers are built through measurable progress.

Long-term ambition becomes practical when it is divided into achievable development goals.

Week 01

Understand the workplace, safety requirements, products, department and reporting structure.

Day 15

Explain the purpose of your role, identify key documents and complete an initial guided assignment.

Month 01

Demonstrate familiarity with recurring processes, systems and professional expectations.

Month 03

Complete defined responsibilities with improving independence and accuracy.

Month 06

Show measurable development in technical knowledge, communication, documentation and problem-solving.

Month 12

Demonstrate dependable role ownership and identify the next stage of technical or professional growth.

← Scroll the timeline →

Goals should remain relevant to the role, measurable wherever possible and reviewed at appropriate intervals.

Chapter 11 · Frequent reviews

Feedback before confusion
becomes a habit.

Professional development should not depend only on an annual performance discussion. Young professionals benefit from timely feedback that helps them understand what they are doing well, what must improve and how they can progress.

Daily

Task coordination and immediate clarification.

Weekly

Work progress and learning discussion.

Monthly

Performance, capability and development review.

Quarterly

Objectives, strengths, improvement areas and future priorities.

Annually

Overall contribution, role development and career direction.

The purpose of evaluation is not to create unnecessary pressure. It is to establish clarity, prevent repeated mistakes and make progress visible.
Chapter 12 · Individual development plans

Think intentionally about your professional growth.

Every fresher enters with a different academic background, level of exposure, learning style and career ambition. An Individual Development Plan may help identify:

Current strengths

What knowledge, skills or behaviours do you already demonstrate confidently?

Role requirements

What capabilities are essential for your current responsibility?

Development areas

Which technical, behavioural, digital or communication skills require improvement?

Immediate goals

What should you understand or perform more effectively during the next three months?

Long-term interests

Which functions, industries, technologies or responsibilities interest you?

Future education

Which certifications, courses or qualifications may support your growth?

Review milestones

When should progress be discussed and objectives updated?

A development plan should guide growth without forcing a young professional into a fixed career direction too early. Interests may evolve as exposure increases.
Chapter 13 · Cross-functional career mobility

Your first department does not have to define your entire career.

A fresher may begin in one function and later discover stronger aptitude in another. Possible career movements may include:

Production → Quality
Quality → Supplier quality
Purchase → Supply chain
Maintenance → Automation
Accounts → Finance
Sales → International business
Marketing → Business development
IT → Digital manufacturing
Data analysis → Operational excellence
Engineering → Project management
Quality → Customer development
Supply chain → Commercial operations

Cross-functional movement should not be treated as escaping a difficult role. It should be approached as a responsible transition towards an area where the individual can create stronger value. Movement depends on performance, capability, qualifications, organisational requirements, appropriate vacancies and a structured handover.

Chapter 16 · Manufacturing and industrial exposure

Understand how individual processes become a complete product.

Fresh engineering and technical professionals may receive relevant exposure to:

Core manufacturing

Wire preparation, cold forging, warm forging, hot forging, thread rolling, nut tapping and precision machining.

Process engineering

Heat treatment, surface finishing, sorting, packaging, production planning and process optimisation.

Tooling and maintenance

Tool design, dies, punches, preventive maintenance, machine reliability and breakdown analysis.

Quality and testing

Incoming inspection, in-process inspection, final inspection, measurement systems, testing and traceability.

Business systems

Purchase, supplier development, planning, inventory, costing, finance, HR, IT and reporting.

Exposure depends on qualifications, role relevance, safety requirements, confidentiality and departmental capacity.

Chapter 17 · Automotive and industrial awareness

See how a component becomes part of a larger system.

Young professionals interested in automobiles, mobility and engineering often begin with the final product. Industrial experience reveals the extensive supplier and manufacturing ecosystem behind every vehicle, machine and engineered assembly. Freshers may develop awareness of:

Engineering fundamentals

Materials, dimensions, tolerances, torque, preload, mechanical properties and product application.

Manufacturing discipline

Process capability, heat treatment, coatings, corrosion protection, productivity and traceability.

Automotive quality

Defect prevention, change control, production approval, documentation, packaging and delivery requirements.

OEM expectations

System-level requirements, delivery performance, quality consistency and customer communication.

Supplier networks

The relationship between OEMs, tier-one suppliers, tier-two suppliers, processors, laboratories and logistics partners.

Every component may appear small individually. Its reliability can influence a much larger system.
Chapter 18 · Quality from the beginning

Quality is not only the responsibility of the quality department.

Quality begins with understanding requirements correctly. It continues through purchasing, tooling, manufacturing, inspection, maintenance, packaging, documentation and delivery. Freshers are expected to learn:

  • Why drawings and specifications must be read carefully
  • Why measurement systems must be reliable
  • Why process deviations must be reported
  • Why traceability matters
  • Why documentation must reflect reality
  • Why defects must be prevented rather than hidden
  • Why corrective actions must address root causes
  • Why changes require review and control
  • Why customer requirements must be respected
  • Why continuous improvement requires evidence
Quality is not a final inspection activity. It is a professional mindset.
Professional conduct

Talent opens the door. Discipline decides how far you go.

Chapter 19 · Professional conduct

Capability builds performance.
Character builds trust.

Professional credibility depends on more than technical knowledge. It is also built through daily behaviour. Freshers are expected to demonstrate:

Integrity

Provide accurate information and communicate mistakes honestly.

Discipline

Respect working hours, deadlines, processes and responsibilities.

Safety

Follow instructions and never compromise workplace safety.

Confidentiality

Protect company, customer, supplier and technical information.

Respect

Value the knowledge, experience and contribution of people across roles.

Accountability

Take responsibility for assigned work and communicate delays early.

Adaptability

Remain open to changing requirements, feedback and new responsibilities.

Collaboration

Support team outcomes rather than focusing only on individual recognition.

Trust is developed when professional behaviour remains consistent, especially when work becomes difficult.
Chapter 20 · Our culture

An environment built around learning, respect and improvement.

Learning

Graduates, experienced professionals and leaders must all continue learning.

Respect

Practical knowledge, academic understanding and responsible conduct are valued across levels.

Quality

Quality is created through coordinated decisions across every department.

Improvement

Evidence-based suggestions and practical solutions are encouraged.

Collaboration

Complex customer requirements are delivered through collective effort.

Integrity

Accuracy, honesty, confidentiality and ethical behaviour are essential.

Opportunity

People are encouraged to develop according to capability, contribution and organisational need.

Internal growth

Training, responsibility and cross-functional exposure can support long-term progression.

Chapter 21 · What we expect

We do not expect years of experience.
We expect a professional attitude.

Mindset

Curiosity, humility, initiative, integrity and openness to feedback.

Discipline

Punctuality, preparation, safety awareness and consistent effort.

Learning

A willingness to ask questions, understand processes and apply guidance.

Contribution

Attention to detail, ownership of assigned work and respect for deadlines.

Communication

Clear updates, responsible escalation and professional workplace interaction.

Improvement

The ability to recognise mistakes, accept correction and avoid repeating them.

Saying, "I do not understand this yet," is not a weakness. Continuing without asking when the work may be incorrect is irresponsible.

Chapter 23 · Fresher opportunity formats

Different beginnings.
One commitment to development.

GET

Graduate Engineer Trainee

For eligible engineering graduates beginning a structured technical and manufacturing career.

DET

Diploma Engineer Trainee

For diploma holders seeking practical responsibility within production, quality, maintenance or related functions.

MT

Management Trainee

FE

Fresher Executive

For entry-level functional positions with clearly defined responsibilities and performance expectations.

TT

Technical Trainee

For candidates developing specialised technical, tooling, testing, maintenance or process capability.

DT

Digital and Technology Trainee

ELP

We look beyond
academic scores alone.

Academic performance may provide useful context, but it is not the only consideration. Applications may be reviewed based on:

  • Relevance of qualification
  • Understanding of the applied role
  • Communication ability
  • Learning attitude
  • Technical fundamentals
  • Problem-solving approach
  • Academic or personal projects
  • Internship or practical exposure
  • Digital capability
  • Professional discipline
  • Career motivation
  • Availability
  • Location and mobility
  • Departmental fit
  • Organisational requirements
  • Suitable vacancies

Selection standards may differ by role. Submission of an application does not guarantee shortlisting, employment or allocation to a preferred department.

Chapter 27 · Application and selection process

From application to professional beginning.

Step 01

Application

Submit the completed form and relevant documents.

Step 02

Initial review

Qualifications, skills, motivation and position relevance are reviewed.

Step 03

Shortlisting

Suitable candidates may be shortlisted for further assessment.

Step 04

Assessment

A technical, aptitude, functional, written or practical assessment may be conducted.

Step 05

Interaction

Shortlisted candidates may participate in an online or in-person discussion.

Step 06

Technical or functional interview

Role knowledge, academic fundamentals, problem-solving and learning capability may be evaluated.

Step 07

Final discussion

Role expectations, availability, location and employment conditions may be discussed.

Step 08

Document verification

Academic, identity and other relevant documents may be reviewed.

Step 09

Offer

Selected candidates receive applicable designation, department, location and joining details.

Step 10

Joining

Employment formalities and required documentation are completed.

Step 11

Orientation

The employee receives organisational, safety and departmental orientation.

Step 12

Goal setting

Initial responsibilities and development objectives are established.

Step 13

Development review

Progress, performance and improvement areas are reviewed during the initial employment period.

Selection steps may vary according to the role, department and number of applicants.

Chapter 28 · Important information

Clear expectations create stronger professional beginnings.

Opportunity availability

Freshers are considered according to suitable vacancies, qualifications and organisational requirements.

Probation or training period

Selected candidates may be required to complete an applicable probation, apprenticeship or training period.

Departmental allocation

Preferences may be considered but cannot be guaranteed.

Work location

Roles may be based at different offices, manufacturing facilities or operational locations.

Working hours

Working schedules may vary according to department and operational requirements.

Safety and confidentiality

Employees must comply with all applicable workplace, safety, information-security and confidentiality requirements.

Performance and continuation

Employment continuation, confirmation, increased responsibility and progression depend on conduct, attendance, capability, performance and organisational requirements.

Career progression

Promotion is not automatic or based only on time served. It depends on sustained contribution, role readiness, available responsibility and organisational requirements.

A message to every beginner

Every professional was once a fresher.

Every engineer once examined a drawing they had never seen before.

Every quality professional once held a measuring instrument without years of experience.

Every manager once completed their first assigned task.

Every expert once asked a basic question.

Every leader once needed someone to recognise their potential.

Your career will not be defined only by the designation with which you begin. It will be shaped by how willing you are to learn, accept responsibility, recover from mistakes, improve your capability and contribute consistently.

Whether your journey begins in Production, Quality, Engineering, Purchase, Finance, Supply Chain, Data Analytics, Human Resources or International Business, each responsibility can become another step towards the professional you choose to become.

Bring your knowledge.
Bring your curiosity.
Bring your discipline.
Bring your ambition.

We will provide an environment in which experience can be built. You must decide what you will build with it.
